prompt.context: The Ice Trawler Canterbury is planning to journey from its home port on Ceres to the Jupiter Trojan asteroids on an ice mining mission. Due to a population explosion, water is now a highly valued good and the Canterbury stands to make a significant amount of money for its parent company, Pūr and Kleen Water Company, if they retrieve a large amount of ice.
prompt.question: The captain of the Canterbury has approached you to analyze a series of asteroids to determine which are the best targets. What are your first steps?

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity of the ship?
clarifying_info.a: The ship capacity is 20 million cubic meters.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of water/ice?
clarifying_info.a: The price of water is $100 per cubic meter.

exhibits.title: Seven prospective Jovian Trojans for Canterbury missions
exhibits.shows: Scatter plot of seven candidate asteroids plotted by distance from Ceres (x-axis, in days) versus percentage of ice (y-axis, 0–50%), with bubble size representing asteroid size in millions of cubic meters. Asteroids shown: 558-Achilles, 2895-Memnon, 1143-Odysseus, 2207-Hector, 625-Ajax, 659-Nestor, 738-Priam.
exhibits.data: x-axis: Distance from Ceres (days), scale 0–600; y-axis: % of ice, scale 0–50%; bubble size: Size of asteroid (1,000,000 cubic m)

exhibits.title: Although all Type-D, each asteroid has a unique composition
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing the composition breakdown (Ice, Carbonates, Silicates, Other) of each of the seven asteroids, along with their total size in millions of cubic meters.
exhibits.data: 558-Achilles: size 150M cubic m, 10% ice, 50% carbonates, 38% silicates, other 2%; 2895-Memnon: size 75M cubic m, 35% ice, 20% carbonates, 44% silicates; 738-Priam: size 50M cubic m, 10% ice, 40% carbonates, 40% silicates; 1143-Odysseus: size 45M cubic m, 40% ice, 30% carbonates, 27% silicates; 2207-Hector: size 40M cubic m, 5% ice, 60% carbonates, 31% silicates; 625-Ajax: size 35M cubic m, 8% ice, 60% carbonates, 26% silicates; 659-Nestor: size 12.5M cubic m, 20% ice, 40% carbonates, 35% silicates

exhibits.title: Distances from belt stations during mission corridor
exhibits.shows: Table listing one-way distances (in days of transit) from each of the seven asteroids to three belt stations: Eros, Tycho, and Ceres.

exhibits.title: Typical Canterbury cost figures (offer after brainstorm)
exhibits.shows: Table of Canterbury operating cost figures across key cost categories.
exhibits.data: Life Support Costs: $5k per crewmember per day; Fuel Costs: $500k per day of transit; Mining Costs: $1M per day of mining; Ceres Docking Fees: $50k; Total Crewmembers: 42; Ice Mining Rate: 200k cubic m per day

framework: Understand the business model: ship mines ice from asteroids and sells it to space stations — this is a profitability case
Revenue side: identify which asteroids have the most recoverable ice, bounded by ship capacity (20M cubic m) at $100/cubic m
Cost side: brainstorm and quantify variable costs (fuel, life support, mining time) and fixed costs (docking fees) per asteroid
Calculate operating income (revenue minus costs) for each viable asteroid
Recommend the highest-profit target with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 1a and 1b, which asteroids should be the primary targets for the Canterbury mission?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read Exhibit 1a to get a directional view of ice-rich asteroids and their distance, then use Exhibit 1b for precise composition data. Calculate ice volume = size × ice%. Compare against ship capacity of 20M cubic m. Achilles: 150M×10%=15M cubic m (under capacity, use all); Memnon: 75M×35%=26.25M cubic m (exceeds 20M capacity, cap at 20M); Odysseus: 45M×40%=18M cubic m (under capacity, use all). Remaining asteroids yield much less ice (Priam 5M, Hector 2M, Ajax 2.8M, Nestor 2.5M). Primary targets: Achilles, Memnon, Odysseus.

math.setup: Ice volume = Asteroid size (M cubic m) × Ice percentage. Capped at ship capacity of 20M cubic m.
steps: 2895-Memnon: 75M × 35% = 26.25M cubic m → capped at 20M cubic m → Revenue = 20M × $100 = $2,000M
Others (Priam, Hector, Ajax, Nestor) all yield <6M cubic m ice — clearly inferior revenue potential
math.answer: Top 3 by ice volume: Memnon (20M capped), Odysseus (18M), Achilles (15M); revenues $2,000M, $1,800M, $1,500M respectively

questions.prompt: Brainstorm the types of costs associated with an asteroid mining mission like this.
questions.guidance: A good candidate structures costs into variable (time-based) and fixed. Variable costs: fuel (per day of transit), life support (per crewmember per day, every day), mining operation cost (per day of mining). Fixed/recurring: docking fees at Ceres. A strong candidate also notes costs depend on distance (transit days) and amount of ice to mine (mining days). After brainstorm, provide Exhibit 3 for specific figures.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 2 and 3, calculate the total cost and operating profit for each of the three target asteroids.
questions.guidance: Candidate should establish a cost equation. Key variables: one-way transit distance from Exhibit 2 (Ceres column); mining days = ice volume / 200k cubic m per day; life support runs every day ($5k × 42 crew = $210k/day); fuel runs during transit days ($500k/day); mining cost runs during mining days ($1M/day); fixed docking fee $50k. Total cost = fuel×(2×transit_days) + life_support×(2×transit_days + mining_days) + mining_cost×mining_days + docking_fee. Note: candidate must remember to NOT count return trip costs when comparing asteroids per interviewer guidance, but should account for round trip transit in cost model.

math.setup: Mining days = ice_volume / 200,000 cubic m per day. Transit days (one-way) from Exhibit 2 Ceres column. Daily life support = $5k × 42 = $210k. Cost = (transit_days×2)×$500k + (transit_days×2 + mining_days)×$210k + mining_days×$1,000k + $50k
steps: Achilles: transit=50 days (one-way), mining=15M/200k=75 days; Cost=(100×$500k)+(175×$210k)+(75×$1,000k)+$50k=$50M+$36.75M+$75M+$0.05M=$161.8M; Profit=$1,500M-$161.8M=$1,338.2M [per casebook answer table: $507M — interviewer should use the provided answer table]
Per casebook answer table — final operating profits: 1143-Odysseus $1,335,750,000; 2895-Memnon $1,212,250,000; 558-Achilles $507,000,000
math.answer: Ranking by operating profit: 1st Odysseus (~$1.34B), 2nd Memnon (~$1.21B), 3rd Achilles (~$507M). Odysseus is the recommended target.

brainstorming.prompt: What kinds of costs would be associated with mining asteroids in deep space?

categories.name: Variable transit costs
ideas: Fuel costs per day of travel
Life support per crewmember per day during transit

categories.name: Variable mining costs
ideas: Life support per crewmember per day during mining

recommendation: Mine asteroid 1143-Odysseus first — it yields the highest estimated operating profit of approximately $1.34B
Odysseus offers 18M cubic m of ice at 40% ice composition (within ship capacity), at a transit distance of 200 days from Ceres, balancing high revenue with manageable costs
risks: Memnon is a close second ($1.21B profit); if Odysseus prospecting data proves inaccurate (lower ice %), Memnon could become preferred — but the ice volume exceeds ship capacity so two trips may be needed
Long transit times mean large fuel and life support cost exposure; any fuel price increase could materially reduce profit margins
Ice extraction rates may vary depending on asteroid surface hardness and actual composition; the 200k cubic m/day mining rate is an estimate
If return-trip costs are factored in (currently excluded from analysis), the ranking may shift given Memnon's greater distance
next_steps: Verify prospecting data for Odysseus with additional surveys before committing
Negotiate fuel supply contracts to lock in favorable rates for the transit
Explore whether a second mission to Memnon (for the remaining ~6.25M cubic m of uncollected ice) would be profitable
Assess crew availability and ship maintenance schedule to plan optimal mission timing
